t: Count Connected Subgraphs with Even Node Sum
o:
We must count non-empty node subsets whose **induced** subgraph is connected and whose value-sum is even. With $n \le 13$ there are at most $2^{13}=8192$ subsets, so enumerating every subset as a bitmask and checking both conditions directly is easily fast enough.

**Example 1** (`nums=[1,0,1]`, path 0-1-2): singletons {0},{2} have odd sum; {1} has even sum but we count it (sum 0 is even) — wait, the table shows [1] counted, giving connected even subsets {1} and {0,1,2}, total **2**. Note {0,2} fails connectivity since the induced subgraph drops edge paths through node 1.

**Example 2**: the only subset {0} has odd sum, so the answer is **0**.

The tiny constraint ($n \le 13$) signals bitmask enumeration; edges up to 78 mean a connectivity check per subset costs at most $O(n+m)$, giving roughly $8192 \times 91$ operations.
k: Represent every subset as an n-bit mask; n ≤ 13 means only 8192 subsets to examine.

Connectivity of an induced subgraph can be tested with BFS/DFS restricted to the mask, or with a subset DP: a mask of size ≥ 2 is connected iff some vertex can be removed leaving a connected mask that still touches it.
The parity of the sum is just the parity of popcount(mask & onesMask), computable in O(1) after preprocessing.

a.n: Approach 1: Enumerate all subsets with BFS connectivity check
a.i: Try every non-empty bitmask. For each mask, compute the value-sum parity by iterating its set bits, then run a BFS/DFS starting from the lowest set bit using a precomputed adjacency bitmask, staying inside the mask. If BFS visits exactly the mask's bits and the sum is even, count it. With n ≤ 13 this brute force is trivially fast.
s: Precompute adj[i] as a bitmask of neighbors of node i.
For each mask m from 1 to 2^n - 1, sum values of set bits; skip if odd.
BFS from the lowest set bit of m, expanding only to neighbors within m.
If all bits of m were visited, increment the answer.
a.t: O(2^n · (n + m)) — each of the 2^n masks triggers an O(n) parity scan plus an O(n + m)-style BFS over bitmask words.
a.sp: O(n + m) — adjacency bitmasks and the BFS stack.

a.i: Avoid re-running BFS per mask with a DP: a mask with ≥ 2 vertices induces a connected subgraph iff there exists a vertex v in it whose removal leaves a connected mask that still contains a neighbor of v (take a leaf of any spanning tree). Computing conn[mask] this way costs O(1) amortized per candidate vertex, giving O(2^n · n) total. Parity is checked via popcount against a precomputed bitmask of value-1 nodes.
s: Build adj bitmasks and onesMask = bitmask of nodes with value 1.
Initialize conn[1 << i] = true for every singleton.
For each mask of size ≥ 2, set conn[mask] = OR over set bits v of (conn[mask ^ v] AND adj[v] intersects mask ^ v).
Add 1 to the answer when conn[mask] holds and popcount(mask & onesMask) is even.
a.t: O(2^n · n) — each mask scans its set bits once for the connectivity transition; parity is O(1) via popcount.
a.sp: O(2^n) — the conn boolean table over all masks.

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1 (it is the natural reading of n ≤ 13), then mention Approach 2 as the asymptotically better refinement if asked to optimize. Pitfalls: forgetting that the induced subgraph drops edges to excluded nodes ({0,2} in Example 1 is disconnected even though a path exists in the full graph); remembering that a sum of 0 is even, so isolated value-0 nodes count; handling empty edge lists and n = 1. Edge cases: no edges at all (answer = number of nodes with value 0), all values 1 (answer counts connected subsets of even size). Follow-ups might ask for larger n (requiring cleverer counting like subtree/Steiner-style DP or generating-function tricks), or counting subsets with sum ≡ k mod m instead of just even.
